reason: Inverting this would let update accept --bootstrap or reject every valid argument list.
The caller would no longer get --bootstrap reported as an unknown argument.
Update would run without a terminal, or be refused inside one.
A missing home directory would no longer give exit code 1.
The restarted program would run a different command instead of update.
Doing the record check first would change what a resumed run reports.
Without an install record, update would continue instead of saying to set up first.
The not-set-up exit code would change.
An unknown newest release would be reported as up to date with exit 0 instead of failing.
A failed lookup would no longer give exit code 1.
Declining would update anyway, or accepting would cancel.
The cancel exit code of update would change.
An update with no trusted key would no longer be refused.
A refused update would no longer give exit code 1.
The failure reason would be printed in the wrong cases or left out.
A failed update would no longer give exit code 1.
An unexpected next state would no longer be reported as failure.
The bootstrap offer would install even when declined.
The cancel exit code of bootstrap would change.
Changes would be applied without asking, or a no-change run would ask.
The 'updated' line would be shown at the wrong time.
Declined changes would be applied anyway.
Declining the changes would give a different exit code.
The skipped-tools heading would show when there are no problems, or be missing when there are.
'Done' would appear after failures or pending steps, or be missing on success.
Computes the result lines from flow state only and writes nothing.
